extracted.intended_audience: journalism/communication researchers, content analysts and advanced students studying news classification and media quality
extracted.subtask_short: classifying news as hard vs soft
extracted.subtask_description: Provide standardized, multi-dimensional definitions and content-analysis coding rules to distinguish ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ news items across topic, focus and style dimensions. Includes concrete coding instructions for political relevance, framing and stylistic indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic / Events dimension (topic as indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most authors use the main topic(s) or subject matter of an item (e.g. politics, economy, sport, culture, celebrities, crime) as an indicator for hard vs soft news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common operationalizations: foreign and domestic politics, economy and finance are usually regarded as hard news; sports, celebrities, royal families, crime, scandals and service are regarded as soft news (De Swert, 2007). Be aware: topic alone can be misleading because the same topic can be framed as politically relevant or as human-interest; code topic separately from focus and style. Studies differ on whether to code one or several topics per item (Scott and Gobetz, 1992 vs Brewer and Marquardt, 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: News production dimension (timeliness / scheduling / urgency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of the journalistic production process used to distinguish hard and soft news, e.g. timeliness, urgent occurrences, need for rapid dissemination or being scheduled vs nonscheduled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-dimensional definitions use timeliness/topicality: Shoemaker and Cohen (2006): 'Hard news items are urgent occurrences that have to be reported right away ... Soft news items (...) are usually based on nonscheduled events. The reporter or media organization is under no pressure to publish the news at a certain date or time – soft news stories need not be ‘timely’.' Note: production attributes are often not directly measurable in content analysis without newsroom data, so they are sometimes omitted or treated cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: News focus dimension — Societal vs Individual relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the report stresses general, societal-level consequences (societal relevance) or personal, private-level consequences/meanings (individual relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding scheme: 0 = pure or predominant focus on individual relevance/consequences; 1 = mixed attention; 2 = pure or predominant focus on societal relevance/consequences. Example: climate change report stressing higher electricity prices (individual) vs required systemic changes (societal). Linkage to public good / policy is an indicator of 'hard' news (Curran et al., 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: News focus dimension — Episodic vs Thematic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a news item presents an issue through a specific example/case (episodic) or places it into broader context, trends, statistics and policy discussion (thematic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding scheme: 0 = pure/predominant episodic framing; 1 = mixed episodic and thematic; 2 = pure/predominant thematic framing. Thematic framing and linkage to public affairs are treated as indicators of harder news; episodic/human-interest framing indicates softer news (Patterson, Baum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Style dimension — Personal vs Impersonal reporting (subjectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a news item includes explicit statements of the reporting journalists’ personal impressions, interpretations, points of view or opinions versus detached factual reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding scheme: 0 = purely or predominantly personal; 1 = mix; 2 = purely or predominantly impersonal. Note: citations of non-author journalists (experts) are not counted as reporter personal opinion. Personalization is an indicator of soft news; impersonal/factual style indicates hard news (Appendix coding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Style dimension — Emotional vs Unemotional reporting (emotionalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a news item uses verbal, visual or auditory means that potentially arouse or amplify emotions among audience members (dramatisation, affective wording, explicit expressions of emotion) versus a matter-of-fact presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding scheme: 0 = purely/predominantly emotional; 1 = mix; 2 = purely/predominantly unemotional. Guidance clarifies that this category is about presentation devices (e.g., dramatizing events, superlatives, present-tense narration, visual emotional cues), not the inherent emotion-arousing potential of the topic itself. Emotionalization is an indicator of softer news (Appendix coding).

rubrics_metrics.name: News reception / effect-related characteristics (entertainment vs public affairs value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience- or effect-related characteristics used in definitions: whether news is experienced as more entertaining, personally useful or interesting (soft) versus more important and informative for understanding public affairs (hard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics are conceptually important but are often not directly coded in content analyses because they concern reception. If included, they require surveys or effect studies. Researchers should be explicit when they include reception criteria and ideally combine content analysis with audience research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-dimensionality principle (combine topic, focus, style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The recommended conceptual principle that hard and soft news should be treated as multi-dimensional constructs made up of combinations of topic, focus and style features rather than a uni-dimensional dichotomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue against one-dimensional definitions and propose standardized, multi-dimensional measurement to improve comparability and cumulative research. Use clusters or scales combining the dimensions instead of relying on single indicators (e.g., timeliness alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political relevance (topic dimension — four-aspect operationalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed content-analysis operationalization indicating the extent to which a news item deals with norms, goals, interests and activities related to authoritative, generally binding decisions about societal issues, using four binary aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code presence (1) or non-presence (0) for each of the four aspects: (1) Two or more societal actors that disagree on a societal issue (e.g., two parties, party and NGO); (2) Decision-making authorities (legislative, executive, judiciary) involved or potentially involved; (3) The substance of a planned or realized decision, measure, programme related to the issue; (4) The persons or groups concerned by the planned or realized decisions/measures/programmes. Sum or treat individually for political relevance assessment (Appendix coding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic coding practice — number and granularity of topic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational choices about how to code topic: length/structure of topic lists, broad vs fine-grained categories, and whether to allow multiple topics per item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should state whether they code one primary topic (Scott and Gobetz) or multiple topics (Brewer and Marquardt), and provide justification. Topic lists vary; be explicit about which topics are pre-assigned to hard or soft and why. Beware implicit assumptions that topic = proxy for societal relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style sub-indicators: sensationalism, visual orientation, vocabulary and ambiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete stylistic indicators used to operationalize style: sensational presentation (described as 'earthshaking/unsettling/remarkable'), visual orientation/visuals, use of superlatives/colloquial vocabulary, dramatization and story ambiance (serious vs light-hearted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code presence/intensity of dramatization, affective wording, present-tense vivid descriptions, explicit visual emotional cues, informal/colloquial language, and sensational adjectives. These indicators support classification as soft/tabloidized/infotainment-style news (Grabe et al., Patterson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing linkage to public good / policy (crime example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationally, judge whether a story links a topic (e.g., crime) to public policy or societal implications (hard) versus reporting the crime itself with details about perpetrators/victims without broader context (soft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contextualization: 'If a crime story was reported in a way that contextualized and linked the issue to the public good – e.g., referred to penal policies or to the general causes or consequences of crime – it was judged to be a hard news story ... If the main focus was the crime itself, with details concerning the perpetrators and victims, but with no reference to the larger context or implications for public policies, ... judged to be soft.' (Curran et al., 2009: 9–10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-dimension definitions (example: topicality-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and capture one-dimensional approaches that classify hard vs soft news solely on a single attribute, typically topicality/timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoemaker and Cohen’s (2006) topicality/timeliness definition is an explicit example and can be used where simplicity or comparability with prior work is desired. If used, state limitations and consider supplementing with other dimensions to capture framing/style differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational limitation: production- and reception-related characteristics hard to measure in content analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that production (newsroom processes, scheduling motives) and reception (audience perceptions/effects) are conceptually part of some definitions but are difficult to infer reliably from content alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If production or reception features are essential to the research question, supplement content analysis with newsroom surveys, participant observation, or audience studies. Otherwise, focus content-analysis on topic, focus and style dimensions that are inferable from the text/visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested minimal standardized instrument (three core coding dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors propose concentrating on three measurable content dimensions—topic (political relevance), focus (individual vs societal; episodic vs thematic) and style (personal vs impersonal; emotional vs unemotional)—as a standardized basis for comparative content analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 and Appendix present this trimmed instrument. Using these core dimensions increases comparability and allows identification of clusters of news items (harder vs softer) across media systems. Researchers should provide coding manuals, reliability tests and report intercoder agreement.
